column2: And Dawn rose from the bed beside lordly Tithonus,
to bring light to the immortals and to mortals;
and the gods sat down in session, and among them
Zeus who thunders on high, whose might is greatest.
To them Athena told the many cares of Odysseus,
remembering him; for it troubled her that he was in the nymph's house:

Father Zeus and you other blessed gods who are for ever,
8	let no sceptre-holding king any longer be willingly
9	kind and gentle, nor know in his mind what is right,
10	but let him always be harsh and do wicked things;
11	since no one remembers godlike Odysseus
12	of the people over whom he ruled, and he was gentle as a father.
13	But he lies on an island suffering mighty pains
14	in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him
15	by force; and he cannot reach his native land;
16	for he has no oared ships and companions
17	who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
18	And now they are eager to kill his beloved child
19	as he comes home; he has gone in search of news of his father
20	to holy Pylos and to divine Lacedaemon.
Answering her, Zeus the cloud-gatherer said:

My child, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth!
23	Did you not yourself devise this plan,
24	that Odysseus will pay them back when he comes?
25	And Telemachus you send with skill, for you can,
26	so that he may reach his native land quite unharmed,
27	and the suitors in their ship may return back again.
He spoke, and to Hermes, his dear son, he said:

Hermes, for you are our messenger in other things as well,
30	tell the fair-tressed nymph my unerring counsel,
31	the return of much-enduring Odysseus, how he is to come home
32	with neither the escort of gods nor of mortal men;
33	but on a raft of many bindings, suffering pains,
34	on the twentieth day he shall reach fertile Scheria,
35	the land of the Phaeacians, who are near to the gods in kin,
36	who will honour him in their hearts like a god,
37	and will send him in a ship to his dear native land,
38	giving him bronze and gold in plenty and clothing,
39	much, as much as Odysseus would never have won from Troy,
40	even if he had come unharmed, having received his share of the spoil.
41	For so it is his fate to see his friends and to reach
42	his high-roofed house and his native land.
So he spoke, and the guide, the slayer of Argus, did not disobey.
At once then he bound beneath his feet the fair sandals,
ambrosial, golden, which carried him over the water
and over the boundless earth with the breath of the wind.
And he took his wand, with which he charms the eyes of men,
whomever he wishes, and others again he wakes from sleep.
Holding it in his hands the strong slayer of Argus flew.
Stepping on Pieria he swooped from the upper air upon the sea;
then he sped over the wave like a sea-gull,
which in the terrible gulfs of the unharvested sea
hunting fish wets its thick wings in the brine;
like it Hermes rode over the many waves.
But when he came to the island that lay afar,
then stepping out of the violet sea onto the land
he went, until he came to the great cave, in which the fair-tressed
nymph dwelt; and he found her inside.
A great fire was burning on the hearth, and far off the smell
of cleft cedar and citron wood was fragrant over the island
as they burned; and she within, singing with a fair voice,
going to and fro by the loom, wove with a golden shuttle.
And a wood grew around the cave, flourishing,
alder and poplar and sweet-smelling cypress.
There long-winged birds roosted,
owls and hawks and long-tongued sea-crows,
who have their business in the sea.
And there around the hollow cave was stretched
a garden vine in its prime, and it was in bloom with grapes.
And springs in a row, four of them, flowed with white water,
near one another, turned each in a different direction.
And around soft meadows of violet and parsley
bloomed. There even an immortal who came
would look and wonder, and be delighted in his heart.
There the guide, the slayer of Argus, stood and wondered.
But when he had wondered at everything in his heart,
at once he went into the wide cave. And face to face
Calypso, bright among goddesses, did not fail to know him when she saw him;
for the immortal gods are not strangers to one another,
not even if one lives in a house far away.
Nor did she find great-hearted Odysseus within,
but he sat weeping on the shore, where he had sat before,
racking his heart with tears and groans and pains.
He kept looking over the unharvested sea, shedding tears.
And Calypso, bright among goddesses, questioned Hermes,
having seated him on a bright, shining chair:

Why, Hermes of the golden wand, have you come to me,
88	revered and dear? Before you did not visit often.
89	Say what you have in mind; my heart bids me accomplish it,
90	if I can accomplish it and if it is a thing that can be accomplished.
91	But follow further in, that I may set before you guest-gifts.
So speaking the goddess set a table
filled with ambrosia, and mixed red nectar.
And the guide, the slayer of Argus, drank and ate.
But when he had dined and refreshed his spirit with food,
then at last he answered her with words and said:

You ask me, a goddess a god, why I have come; and I
98	will tell you the word truly; for you bid me.
99	Zeus ordered me to come here, unwilling;
100	who would willingly run over so much salt water,
101	unspeakable? And no city of mortals is near, who
102	perform sacrifices to the gods and choice hecatombs.
103	But it is in no way possible to pass by or to frustrate
104	the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus, for another god.
105	He says that a man is with you, the most wretched of others,
106	of the men who fought around the city of Priam
107	for nine years, and in the tenth sacked the city and went
108	home; but on the return they sinned against Athena,
109	who raised against them an evil wind and long waves.
110	There all the other good companions perished,
111	but him wind and wave bore and brought near here.
112	Him he now bids you send away as quickly as possible;
113	for it is not his fate to perish here far from his friends,
114	but it is still his fate to see his friends and to reach
115	his high-roofed house and his native land.
So he spoke, and Calypso, bright among goddesses, shuddered,
and speaking to him she addressed him with winged words:

You are cruel, gods, jealous beyond all others,
119	who begrudge goddesses sleeping with men
120	openly, if one makes a man her dear husband.
121	So when rosy-fingered Dawn took Orion,
122	you gods who live easily begrudged her,
123	until in Ortygia pure Artemis of the golden throne
124	came upon him with her gentle shafts and killed him.
125	And so when fair-tressed Demeter, yielding
126	to her heart, mingled in love and bed with Iasion
127	in a thrice-ploughed fallow field; and not long was it unheard of by
128	Zeus, who killed him, striking him with a white thunderbolt.
129	So now again you begrudge me, gods, a mortal man beside me.
130	Him I saved, as he bestrode the keel
131	alone, when Zeus with a white thunderbolt struck
132	and shattered his swift ship in the midst of the wine-dark sea.
133	There all the other good companions perished,
134	but him wind and wave bore and brought near here.
135	Him I loved and nurtured, and I said that I would
136	make him immortal and ageless all his days.
137	But since it is in no way possible to pass by or to frustrate
138	the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus, for another god,
139	let him go, if that man urges and bids it,
140	over the unharvested sea; but I will not send him anywhere myself;
141	for I have no oared ships and companions
142	who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
143	But I will readily advise him, and will not hide it,
144	how he may reach his native land quite unharmed.
Then again the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to her:

So send him away now, and respect the wrath of Zeus,
147	lest in anger he be harsh to you hereafter.
So speaking the strong slayer of Argus departed;
and the queenly nymph went to great-hearted Odysseus,
when she had heard the messages of Zeus.
Him she found sitting on the shore; and never were his eyes
dry of tears, and his sweet life was ebbing away
as he mourned his return, since the nymph no longer pleased him.
But by night he would sleep, by compulsion,
in the hollow caves, unwilling beside her willing;
and by day, sitting on the rocks and the beaches,
racking his heart with tears and groans and pains,
he kept looking over the unharvested sea, shedding tears.
And standing near, the bright one among goddesses spoke to him:

Ill-fated man, no longer lament here, and do not let your life
161	waste away; for already I will send you off most readily.
162	But come, cutting long timbers fit together with bronze
163	a broad raft; and fasten a deck upon it
164	high up, that it may carry you over the misty sea.
165	And I will put in bread and water and red wine,
166	satisfying things, which may keep hunger from you,
167	and I will clothe you; and I will send a wind behind you,
168	that you may reach your native land quite unharmed,
169	if the gods are willing, who hold the broad heaven,
170	who are stronger than I to plan and to accomplish.
So she spoke, and much-enduring godlike Odysseus shuddered,
and speaking to her he addressed her with winged words:

Something else, goddess, you are devising by this, and not at all a sending-off,
174	you who bid me cross the great gulf of the sea on a raft,
175	terrible and painful; which not even balanced ships
176	swift-faring cross, rejoicing in the wind of Zeus.
177	Nor would I go aboard a raft against your will,
178	unless you, goddess, will bring yourself to swear a great oath for me
179	that you will not devise some other evil harm against me myself.
So he spoke, and Calypso, bright among goddesses, smiled,
and stroked him with her hand, and spoke a word and called him by name:

Truly you are a rogue and not without knowing mischief,
183	what a word you have thought to utter!
184	Let earth know this now, and the broad heaven above,
185	and the down-flowing water of Styx, which is the greatest
186	and most terrible oath for the blessed gods,
187	that I will not devise some other evil harm against you yourself.
188	But I am thinking and will devise such things as I would
189	plan for myself, when such need should come upon me;
190	for I too have a just mind, and my own
191	heart in my breast is not of iron, but pitying.
So speaking, the bright one among goddesses led the way
swiftly; and he then followed in the footsteps of the goddess.
And they came to the hollow cave, the goddess and the man,
and he sat down on the chair from which Hermes had risen,
and the nymph set beside him all kinds of food,
to eat and to drink, such as mortal men eat;
and she herself sat opposite godlike Odysseus,
and the maids set ambrosia and nectar beside her.
And they stretched out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
But when they had taken their fill of food and drink,
then Calypso, bright among goddesses, began to speak among them:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
204	so then to your home, to your dear native land
205	you wish to go at once now? Yet farewell to you all the same.
206	But if you knew in your mind how many troubles
207	fate has for you to fill up before you reach your native land,
208	you would stay here again with me and keep this house
209	and be immortal, though you long to see
210	your wife, for whom you yearn all your days.
211	Surely I do not claim to be worse than she,
212	neither in form nor in stature, since it is in no way fitting
213	for mortals to rival immortals in form and appearance.
Answering her, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Queenly goddess, do not be angry with me for this; I know myself
216	very well that prudent Penelope is
217	less than you in appearance and in stature to look upon;
218	for she is mortal, and you are immortal and ageless.
219	But even so I wish and long all my days
220	to go home and to see the day of return.
221	And if some god strikes me on the wine-dark sea,
222	I will endure it, having in my breast a heart that bears sorrows;
223	for already I have suffered very much and toiled much
224	in waves and in war; let this too be added to those.
So he spoke, and the sun set and darkness came on;
and going into the inner part of the hollow cave
the two took pleasure in love, staying beside one another.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
at once Odysseus put on a cloak and tunic,
and the nymph herself put on a great silvery robe,
fine and graceful, and cast about her waist
a fair golden girdle, and a veil on her head above.
And then she planned a sending-off for great-hearted Odysseus:
she gave him a great axe, fitting his hands,
of bronze, sharpened on both sides; and in it
was a very beautiful handle of olive-wood, well fitted;
then she gave him a well-polished adze; and she led the way
to the edge of the island, where tall trees grew,
alder and poplar and fir that reached to heaven,
dry long since, well-seasoned, which would float lightly for him.
But when she had shown him where the tall trees grew,
Calypso, bright among goddesses, went to her house,
and he cut timbers; and quickly his work was done.
Twenty in all he felled, and trimmed them with bronze,
and smoothed them skilfully and made them straight to the line.
Meanwhile Calypso, bright among goddesses, brought augers;
and he bored all of them and fitted them to one another,
and with pegs and joints he hammered it together.
As wide as a man who is well skilled in carpentry
marks out the floor of a broad freighter,
so wide a broad raft did Odysseus make.
And setting up the deck, fitting it with close-set ribs,
he built; and he finished it with long side-planks.
And in it he made a mast and a yard-arm fitted to it;
and besides he made a steering-oar, that he might steer.
And he fenced it all along with willow withies,
to be a defence against the wave; and he threw in much brushwood.
Meanwhile Calypso, bright among goddesses, brought cloth
for making sails; and he made these skilfully too.
And in it he fastened braces and halyards and sheets,
and with levers he drew it down into the divine sea.
It was the fourth day, and everything was finished for him;
and on the fifth, bright Calypso sent him from the island,
having bathed him and clothed him in fragrant garments.
And the goddess put in it a skin of dark wine,
one, and another great one of water, and food too
in a leather bag; and she put in many satisfying meats;
and she sent a wind, harmless and gentle.
And glad at the wind godlike Odysseus spread his sails.
And he steered skilfully with the steering-oar,
sitting, and sleep did not fall upon his eyelids
as he watched the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes
and the Bear, which they also call the Wain by name,
which turns in the same place and watches Orion,
and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean;
for this one Calypso, bright among goddesses, had bidden him
keep on his left hand as he sailed over the sea.
Seventeen days he sailed, voyaging over the sea,
and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains appeared
of the land of the Phaeacians, where it lay nearest to him;
and it showed like a shield in the misty sea.
But him, returning from the Ethiopians, the lord Earth-shaker
saw from afar from the mountains of the Solymi; for he appeared to him
sailing on the sea. And he was angered still more in his heart,
and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:

Oh dear, truly the gods have changed their minds otherwise
287	about Odysseus while I was among the Ethiopians,
288	and now he is near the land of the Phaeacians, where it is his fate
289	to escape the great end of misery that has come upon him.
290	But still I say I will drive him to his fill of evil.
So saying he gathered the clouds, and stirred up the sea,
taking the trident in his hands; and he roused all the gales
of all kinds of winds, and covered with clouds
land and sea together; and night rushed down from heaven.
East and South together fell upon it, and ill-blowing West,
and North, born in the upper air, rolling a great wave.
And then the knees and dear heart of Odysseus were loosed,
and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-hearted spirit:

Ah me, wretched man, what will at last become of me?
300	I fear that the goddess has told all things truly,
301	who said that on the sea, before I reach my native land,
302	I should fill up my pains; and now all this is being fulfilled.
303	With what clouds Zeus crowns the broad heaven,
304	and has stirred up the sea, and gales rush on
305	of all kinds of winds. Now for me sheer destruction is certain.
306	Thrice blessed the Danaans and four times, who then perished
307	in wide Troy bringing favour to the sons of Atreus.
308	So I wish that I had died and met my fate
309	on that day when the most Trojans threw bronze-tipped spears
310	about me, when Achilles was dead.
311	I would have got funeral rites, and the Achaeans would have spread my fame;
312	but now it was fated for me to be caught by a miserable death.
So he spoke, and a great wave struck down on him from above,
terribly rushing, and whirled the raft around.
Far from the raft he himself fell, and the steering-oar
he let go from his hands; and his mast in the middle
a terrible blast of mingled winds that came broke,
and far off the sail and yard fell into the sea.
Him under water it held for a long time, nor could he
quickly lift himself up from beneath the force of the great wave;
For the clothes weighed him down, which bright Calypso had given him.
At last he came up, and spat from his mouth the bitter
brine, which ran down in streams from his head.
But even so he did not forget the raft, wearied though he was,
but, springing after it amid the waves, he seized it,
and sat in the middle, avoiding the end of death.
And the great wave carried it with the current this way and that.
As when the autumn North Wind carries thistles
over the plain, and they cling thick to one another,
so the winds carried it over the sea this way and that;
at one time the South would throw it to the North to carry,
and at another the East would yield it to the West to chase.
But the daughter of Cadmus saw him, fair-ankled Ino,
Leucothea, who before was a mortal with human speech,
but now in the depths of the sea has her share of honour from the gods.
She pitied Odysseus wandering, having pains,
and in the form of a sea-gull she rose from the water in flight,
and sat on the raft of many bindings and spoke a word:

Ill-fated man, why is Poseidon the Earth-shaker so
340	terribly angry with you, that he plants so many evils for you?
341	He will not destroy you, though he rages greatly.
342	But do this, and you seem to me not to be senseless:
343	stripping off these clothes, leave the raft to be carried by the winds,
344	and swim with your hands and strive for a return
345	to the land of the Phaeacians, where it is your fate to escape.
346	Here, stretch this immortal veil beneath your chest;
347	and there is no fear for you of suffering or perishing.
348	But when you take hold of the mainland with your hands,
349	loosing it again, throw it into the wine-dark sea
350	far from the mainland, and turn yourself away.
So speaking the goddess gave him the veil,
and herself plunged again into the surging sea
like a sea-gull; and a dark wave covered her.
But he pondered, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
and, troubled, spoke to his own great-hearted spirit:

Ah me, lest some one of the immortals weave a trick again
357	for me, bidding me leave the raft.
358	But I will not yet obey, since with my eyes I saw
359	the land far off, where she said it was an escape for me.
360	But I will do this, and it seems to me to be best:
361	as long as the timbers remain fitted in their joints,
362	so long I will stay here and endure, suffering pains;
363	but when the wave shatters my raft,
364	I will swim, since there is nothing better to plan beforehand.
While he was pondering this in his mind and in his heart,
Poseidon the Earth-shaker raised a great wave,
terrible and grievous, arching over, and drove it at him.
As when a strong wind shakes a heap of dry chaff,
and it scatters some this way and some that,
so it scattered the long timbers of the raft. But Odysseus
mounted on one timber, riding it as a horse,
and stripped off the clothes which bright Calypso had given him.
At once he stretched the veil beneath his chest,
and himself fell face down into the sea, stretching out his hands,
eager to swim. And the lord Earth-shaker saw him,
and shaking his head spoke to his own heart:

So now, having suffered many evils, wander over the sea,
378	until you mingle with Zeus-nurtured men.
379	But even so I do not think you will make light of your misery.
So speaking he lashed his fair-maned horses,
and came to Aegae, where he has his famous halls.
But Athena, daughter of Zeus, thought of another thing.
She bound the paths of the other winds,
and bade them cease and all go to sleep;
and she roused the swift North Wind, and broke the waves before him,
until he should mingle with the Phaeacians, lovers of oars,
Zeus-born Odysseus, having escaped death and the dooms.
There for two nights and two days on the heavy swell
he drifted, and his heart often foresaw destruction.
But when fair-tressed Dawn brought the third day to its end,
then the wind ceased, and there was a windless
calm; and he looked on the land close by,
looking forward very sharply, lifted by a great wave.
As when the life of a father appears welcome to his children,
who lies in sickness suffering mighty pains,
wasting a long time, and some hateful deity has fallen on him,
and gladly the gods have loosed him from his misery,
so welcome to Odysseus appeared land and forest,
and he swam on, hastening to set foot on the mainland.
But when he was as far off as a man's shout carries,
and now he heard the din of the sea against the reefs;
for the great wave roared against the dry land,
terribly belching, and all was wrapped in the sea-spray;
for there were no harbours holding ships, nor roadsteads,
but projecting headlands, and reefs and crags.
And then the knees and dear heart of Odysseus were loosed,
and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-hearted spirit:

Ah me, since Zeus has given me to see a land beyond hope,
409	and I have cut through this gulf and crossed it,
410	no way out appears anywhere from the grey sea to the shore;
411	for outside are sharp crags, and around them the wave
412	roars and rushes, and a smooth rock runs up,
413	and the sea is deep close in, and there is no way to
414	stand on both feet and escape from misery;
415	lest as I come out the great wave seize and dash me
416	against the stony rock; and my effort will be wretched.
417	But if I swim along still further, in case I may find
418	sloping beaches and harbours of the sea,
419	I fear that a storm-wind may seize me again
420	and carry me over the fishy sea, groaning heavily,
421	or a deity may even send a great monster against me
422	from the sea, such as famous Amphitrite breeds in numbers;
423	for I know how the famous Earth-shaker is angry with me.
While he was pondering this in his mind and in his heart,
meanwhile a great wave carried him to the rugged shore.
There his skin would have been stripped and his bones crushed,
had not grey-eyed Athena put a thought in his mind:
rushing on he seized the rock with both his hands,
and clung to it groaning, until the great wave passed by.
And that one he so escaped, but the back-flowing wave
struck him again as he rushed, and threw him far into the sea.
As when from the chamber of a polyp being dragged out
thick pebbles cling to its suckers,
so from his bold hands against the rocks
the skin was stripped away; and the great wave covered him.
There wretched Odysseus would have perished beyond his fate,
had not grey-eyed Athena given him presence of mind.
Rising out of the wave which belches toward the mainland,
he swam along outside, looking toward the land, in case he might find
sloping beaches and harbours of the sea.
But when swimming he came to the mouth of a fair-flowing river,
there the place seemed best to him,
smooth of rocks, and there was shelter from the wind,
and he knew it as it flowed out, and prayed in his heart:

Hear me, lord, whoever you are; much entreated I come to you,
446	fleeing from the sea, from the threats of Poseidon.
447	Revered even to the immortal gods is
448	any man who comes wandering, as I too now
449	come to your stream and your knees after much toil.
450	But pity me, lord; I declare myself your suppliant.
So he spoke, and the river at once stopped its flow, and held back the wave,
and made a calm before him, and saved him
at the river's mouth. And he bent both knees
and his stout hands. For his heart was overcome by the sea.
And all his flesh was swollen, and sea-water gushed much
from his mouth and nostrils; and he lay breathless and speechless,
faint, and terrible weariness came upon him.
But when he drew breath and his spirit gathered in his heart,
then he loosed from himself the veil of the goddess.
And he let it go into the salt-flowing river,
and the great wave bore it back down the stream, and at once Ino
received it in her dear hands. And he, withdrawing from the river,
sank down in the reeds, and kissed the grain-giving earth.
And troubled he spoke to his own great-hearted spirit:

Ah me, what shall I suffer? What will at last become of me?
466	If I keep a miserable night watch by the river,
467	lest the evil frost and the female dew together
468	overcome my gasping spirit in my faintness;
469	and a cold breeze blows from the river before dawn.
470	But if I climb the slope to the shady wood
471	and sleep in the thick bushes, if the cold
472	and weariness leave me and sweet sleep comes upon me,
473	I fear that I may become prey and spoil for wild beasts.
So as he thought, this seemed to him to be better;
he went to the wood; and he found it near the water
in an open place; and he went under two bushes,
growing from one spot, one of wild olive, one of olive.
Through these neither did the strength of the moist-blowing winds pass,
nor did the shining sun ever strike them with its rays,
nor did rain pass through; so thick
they had grown, interwoven with one another; under them Odysseus
crept. And at once he heaped up with his dear hands a broad bed;
for there was an abundance of fallen leaves,
enough to shelter two or three men
in winter-time, even if it were very harsh.
Seeing it, much-enduring godlike Odysseus rejoiced,
and lay down in the middle, and heaped a pile of leaves over himself.
As when someone hides a brand in black ashes
at the edge of a field, where no other neighbours are near,
saving a seed of fire, so that he need not kindle it from elsewhere,
so Odysseus covered himself with leaves; and Athena
poured sleep on his eyes, that it might quickly end
his toilsome weariness, having covered his dear eyelids.
